ENGINEERING AND 
COMMUNICATION

Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry o f Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 231-277
Structural Assessment of Maitri Building 
at Antarctica
G. Raghava & S.G.N. Murthy
Structural Engineering Research Centre, Chennai
ABSTRACT
Structural assessment of Maitri building in Antarctica was carried out by two 
scientists of SERC during the XXIIIIAE. This report gives the details of work 
carried out, defects, damage and deterioration found in the structure, and 
observations made during the study.
Thickness measurement of supporting columns was made by using an 
ultrasonic thickness gauge. The measurements show fairly uniform readings 
throughout the structure. No drastic localised reduction of thickness was observed 
anywhere in the columns. This rule out any localised excessive corrosion of the 
members. During visual examination of the supporting structure, cracks were 
identified in nine supporting columns. Length of crack in the supporting columns 
of the main block varies from 7 cm to 50 cm and extends below ground level in some 
columns. It is physically seen that some cracks are through-thickness cracks for 
part of the length. An evaluation of safety of cracked columns and possible repair 
measure is included. Blocks A and C of the station warrant immediate replacement. 
Reasons for the same have been explained in the report with photographs. Other 
observations made during the structural assessment have also been given in the 
report. Data of acceleration obtained from Maitri during gusty winds have been 
analysed using FFT and acceleration spectrum has been obtained. It is noted that 
the data obtained are not adequate to determine the wind sensitivity of the structure. 
A thorough investigation with measurements at higher wind speeds is necessary.
INTRODUCTION
India launched its first scientific expedition to Antarctica in the year 
1981. The first permanent station ‘Dakshina Gangotri’  was established during 
the third expedition in the year 1983-84. This station was located at 70°05’  
South Latitude and 12°00’  East Longitude on ice shelf on Princess Astrid 
coast. The thickness of ice shelf is reported to be 150 m in this region. The 
site is reasonably close to the ice-shelf edge (1). Dakshina Gangotri got 
buried under accumulated snow over years and was abandoned in the year 
1990-91. In the year 1989, a new permanent station ‘M aitri’  was

232 G . Raghava & S. G.N. Murthy
commissioned. Maitri lies at the ‘Schirmacher Region’  of east Antarctica at 
70°45’58" South Latitude and 11°43’56" East Longitude (2). This is an ice- 
free mountainous terrain where the problem of permanent accumulation of 
drifting snow does not exist. There is a lake called ‘Priyadarshini’  in the 
vicinity of the station. In the last 15 years, around 370 scientists, technicians, 
and officers and other personnel from the army and navy have over-wintered 
safely and successfully in this station. Presently, 25 members from 9 different 
organizations are over-wintering in this station.
As against the original design life of ten years, Maitri has already 
served as a permanent station of the Indian scientists for the last fifteen 
years. Because of some damage observed in the structure and also because 
of the fact that the structure has already completed fifteen years of service 
as against the design life of ten years, Structural Engineering Research 
Centre (SERC), Chennai was asked to carry out ‘Structural assessment of 
the Maitri building in Antarctica’.  G. Raghava and S.G.N. Murthy, Scientists 
from SERC, participated as team members of the XXIII Indian Scientific 
Expedition to Antarctica and carried out the structural assessment of the 
Maitri Structure. They were a part of the expedition team during December
2003 -  April 2004. They actually stayed in the summer camp huts in the 
Maitri region during January and February 2004 and carried out the structural 
assessment.
. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVES OF THE PROJECT
The following were the scope and objectives of the project:
• Detailed visual examination of the structure, identification of 
locations which require further detailed inspection/examination
• Collection of samples of the materials used in the construction of 
the structure and collection of any other relevant data and 
information relevant to the structure
• Collection of data from accelerometers using impact hammer 
technique
• Preparation of report giving details of the condition assessment 
of the existing structure, analysis/interpretation of results of various 
measurements and recommendations to improve/strengthen the 
existing structure if feasible.
